awd_titl_txt: Conference: Macaulay2 Workshop at Tulane University
awd_abstract_narration:
This award supports the “Macaulay2 Workshop at Tulane University,” which will be held at Tulane University from April 14-18, 2025. This week-long intensive workshop will be focused on the development of the free and open-source computer algebra software system Macaulay2, which is widely used for research in commutative algebra and algebraic geometry. The workshop aims to develop research infrastructure through the creation and maintenance of Macaulay2 packages, to train early-career researchers in the use and development of the software system, and to facilitate collaborations. It will include a two-day mini-school providing training for participants new to Macaulay2. The workshop also encourages the formation of research communities among graduate students through scheduled lightning talks and a networking event. 

The specific software development goals are motivated by current needs in active mathematical research areas. Participants will contribute to Macaulay2 packages that implement algorithms and constructions from the invariant theory of tensors and auxiliary algebras, the computation of invariants of linearly reductive groups, injective resolutions in topological data analysis, Gaussian mixture models, and subvarieties under birational maps relevant to algebraic statistics. The conference website is https://sites.google.com/view/macaulay2tulane/.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Modern mathematics increasingly depends on software. Macaulay2 is a free, open-source program that mathematicians around the world use to explore problems in algebra and geometry, the study of equations and the shapes they describe. Its power comes from a community of researchers who build and share new tools for it. This award supported a week-long workshop at Tulane University in New Orleans, where that community came together to expand the software and to train the next generation of people who will use and improve it.

Intellectual Merit

About 60 mathematicians, from undergraduates and graduate students to senior researchers, took part, and more than 45 of them traveled from outside the city. They worked in six project teams, each led by an experienced researcher, and the work produced concrete results:

One team added specialized, much faster methods for a common kind of symmetry to a package for computing invariants, quantities that stay unchanged when an object is transformed. Members of this team also helped develop a new method for another family of symmetries. It is now included in the latest Macaulay2 release and described in a research paper.
A second team created a package called PowerSums that solves certain systems of equations arising from Gaussian mixture models, a standard statistical tool for analyzing data drawn from several overlapping groups. A research paper is in progress.
A third team wrote most of a new package for rigidity theory. It is being documented for publication in a software journal.
A fourth team extended a package for representations of Lie algebras, a mathematical language used to describe symmetry in both mathematics and physics. It became part of the official Macaulay2 distribution, and a research paper based on calculations with it has since been posted.
Two further teams built software for Young tableaux, combinatorial diagrams that arise throughout algebra, and for the algebra of tensors. One team’s work is being merged with a related package.

All of the code produced is publicly available, so any researcher can use it and build on it.

Broader Impacts

The workshop was also designed to train people. A two-day mini-school introduced about 30 newcomers to Macaulay2, so they could contribute to real research projects from the start rather than watching from the sidelines. Eleven junior participants gave short “lightning talks” about their own work, which let them practice public speaking and meet senior researchers working in related areas. A networking lunch and end-of-week project presentations added more chances to build skills and professional connections.

Because Macaulay2 is free and open source, the benefits reach well beyond the people in the room. The new tools are freely available to researchers in mathematics, computer science, statistics, and other fields that rely on computation with equations. The newly trained participants can carry what they learned into their own research, classrooms, and collaborations, strengthening the community that keeps this shared scientific resource growing.
